utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Yes, Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, everyone in the courtroom. May I introduce Ms. Sarah Coquillaud who has been assisting my team. She's now on her second internship with us, having in the interim gone to the ICC, but having decided it was better to come back and work with us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Welcome back. Good morning, Mr. Dzino. Yes, Mr. Gaynor, good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Dzino. Mr. Dzino, the first question is --

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Concerns who took your statement. Could you identify the members of the Defence team who took your statement?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember the name. Danko, Danko is the name, or rather, it's last name. I can't remember Kostovic, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Anybody else?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: All right. In your statement at paragraph 3 you said that you were a guard in the village of Bojnik in Rajlovac municipality from the 1st of March until the end of -- the 29th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before we proceed. Mr. Dzino, do you have your statement with you now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you like to have one in hard copy, Mr. Dzino? Or you have it in your bag?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes -- no, I forgot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll print it out for you. Yes, it's on the monitor, if you could take a look there. Yes, please continue, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: My question is: Did the guard in the village of Bojnik operate under the authority of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, as I was a little bit distracted here. Could you tell me which period you are referring to. I also don't have the statement before me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: It's in paragraph 3 in front of you. You said that from the 1st of March until the 29th of May, 1992, you acted as a guard in the village of Bojnik.

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Did the guard in the village of Bojnik operate under the authority of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Perhaps I should go into detail. From the 2nd of March barricades were set up in Sarajevo, and as of that time there was a lot of tension and all the inhabitants in our commune were nervous, Serbs, Muslims, and Croats. So from the time the barricades were set up the Serbs, the Croats, and the Muslims went on guard duty, everyone did. There wasn't a unit of -- the unit wasn't armed. They had perhaps hunting rifles and so on and so forth, but the guards were set up in front of people's houses. No one obstructed anyone else. There were no attacks or provocations or anything of that kind. So that's how it was in the beginning. Later in May --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Dzino, if you could concentrate on answering the question. The question was whether the guard operated under the authority of the Crisis Staff. If you didn't know, that's sufficient. Do you understand that, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellent. So in March and April I wasn't aware of being under anyone's orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, you say that you were securing the village as platoon commander. Is it correct that you were the Rajlovac platoon commander?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, but I became the platoon commander on the 26th of May, 1992. Up until that point in time we didn't have an established unit with its commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Okay. So you're saying that before the 26th of May, 1992, there was no Rajlovac platoon commander; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not in Rajlovac. Are you asking me? I have no idea about what happened in Rajlovac, but -- in my local commune. But we're talking about Mihaljevici, Bojnik, part of the local commune.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Can I call up, please, P2329.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: The document that's coming up is a little hard to read, we can see, but it appears to be dated the 9th of the 4th, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'll have the English translation amended because it does appear to say the 9th of the 4th rather than the 1st of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, this appears, does it not, to be an order of the Crisis Staff of the Rajlovac municipality, Mr. Dzino? Can you confirm that that is an order of the Crisis Staff of the Rajlovac municipality?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here it says it's an order, but I can tell you that we did not abide by this. It was on the 26th of March -- 26th of May, 1992. You have my diary where it says when the platoon was formed and when I became its commander. So I didn't receive an order, a written order, of any kind. Things proceeded a little more slowly in our case, and as you can see it was only one month later, over one month later, that we established a unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: But do you agree that according to point 1 of this order, the active observation of the entire territory of Rajlovac municipality is ordered?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And it orders platoon commanders and Crisis Staffs are to be informed on everything noticed?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether you understand what I'm saying. It was on the 26th of May. We said that the date here is the 9th of April. If that is the case, 21, 26, that's 47 days later that I became the platoon commander. Is that clear to you? And as proof, I have my diary that you also have at your disposal, so please feel free to read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: All right. But this document does fall within the period during which you were performing guard duties in the village of Bojnik, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't received any interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you repeat.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: This document, this order from the Rajlovac municipality Crisis Staff, dated the 9th of April, 1992, does fall within the period between the 1st of March and the end of May 1992 when you were performing guard duties.

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, but are you asking me whether I was the platoon commander or not? I don't know what your question is. Could you repeat your question. Naturally this is an order, but I was the platoon commander from the 26th of May, 1992. So this order does not concern me. I'm only concerned as of the 26th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And your platoon did act in co-operation with the Crisis Staff, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It started acting from the 26th of May. Up until that time - I don't know whether you understand what I'm saying - but up until that point in time all we had were village guards that were poorly organised. They would all stand guard in front of their houses at night, whereas during the day they would till the land. We lived in a village and we tilled the land, we worked. No one launched any attacks during the day. There were no provocations of any kind. Provocations were carried out at night. Some would open fire in one location. It was only on the 26th of May, 1992, that a platoon was established and I was appointed as commander of the platoon by the soldiers, the soldiers who were with me. And if we're dealing with the platoon you can ask me about that, but up until that point in time I wasn't in command of anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I want to move now to the establishment of the municipality of Rajlovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could I call up, please, P2315.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, as you can see, this is taken from the Official Gazette of the Republika Srpska of 24th February 1993 and it is reproducing a decree of the 15th of May, 1992, issued by the president of the Presidency, Dr. Radovan Karadzic. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO [Resumed]
utterances.text: This decree, is that it?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, it's the --

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not very legible -- now it's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: If we move a little down we see the law on the establishment of Rajlovac municipality with headquarters in Rajlovac. As you can see at the end of that, that that was issued. If we go to the next page in English, it was issued by the president of the Assembly of the Serbian people, Momcilo Krajisnik, on the 11th of May, 1992. And you see that portion of the document, Mr. Dzino?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 5 of your statement, if we can return to the first page in English, please, in paragraph 5 of your statement you say that the local commune of Dobrosevici comprised the villages of Bojnik, Mihaljevici, Dobrosevici, and Ahatovici; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well -- and the question is?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, if you look at Article 2 of the law, it identifies the territorial extent of Sarajevo Rajlovac municipality and it encompasses the following populated areas, including Bojnik, Dobrosevici, Ahatovici, and it goes on to list a number of other settlements in that area. You see that?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: So is it correct to say that the local commune of Dobrosevici was incorporated within the municipality of Rajlovac?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And that includes the 1.066 Muslims and 200 Croats who were living there according to the 1991 census?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, do you know if they were ever consulted about the incorporation of their commune into the municipality of Rajlovac?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, yesterday in your evidence you confirmed that the surrender of Muslim civilians from Ahatovici to Serb forces was on the 2nd of June, 1992, and they were taken away. That was at pages 2857 and 2 -- sorry, excuse me. That was at pages 29857 and 29858. Now, do you know the mosque at Ahatovici?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: It was built in about 1969; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know when, but I know that there was a mosque. I don't know the year in which it was built, but I know that there was a mosque.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And do you know what happened to it in 1992?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: What happened?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you want me to describe the case to you ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Well, it was blown up, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, the Trial Chamber's received evidence that it was destroyed sometime after the Serb take-over of Ahatovici which you've placed at the 2nd of June, 1992, and before the 6th of June, 1992. Do you have any reason to dispute that?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know all the details about the mosque being blown up, but I watched this. It was on the 4th when I read through my diary -- in fact, I haven't noted anything here. But I reminded myself by reading through Ramiz Mujkic's statement, a neighbour of mine who was here before me. I reminded myself of the date on which this occurred. It was on the 4th of June and at the time Ahatovici had not been taken. Because on the 4th of June, Serbian forces had taken control of Ahatovici for good, so that was in the course of combing the field. It was a terrible explosion. I saw it from a distance of 1 kilometre. If you want me to tell you anything else about this case, please tell me to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, who -- it was blown up by the Serb forces, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't say that they blew it up because I don't know the details, but rumour had it that there were some ammunition in the mosque, some explosives, or that it had been hit by a heavy-calibre weapon and it exploded, it was blown up, it was like an atom bomb. There was a lot of smoke. The mosque is in a valley. I was at an elevation 1 kilometre away, so the scene was quite appalling.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Did you personally ever see ammunition --

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was as if a rocket had been fired.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Did you personally ever see any ammunition in the mosque?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise for the expression, but, Mr. Prosecutor, it's a ridiculous question. This happened ... the ammunition was hidden when we weren't there. We were taking Ahatovici when the mosque exploded, so no one could see what you are suggesting. But given the force of the explosion, the detonation, smoke, and so on and so forth, we could conclude that there was something in it. I don't know what it was, I am not an expert for explosives and do not understand these matters.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to comment on the transcript. It doesn't say that the witness said he didn't see them bringing the ammunition into the mosque, but they drew this conclusion on the basis of the explosions. They couldn't see that because the Serbs were not in Ahatovici at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, I ask the CLSS to look into the response of the witness later on. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: So essentially, it was a mere rumour that there had been explosives in the mosque and you deduced from the size of the explosion that there had been ammunition stored in the mosque. You never saw any ammunition there yourself, did you?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, who provided the statement of Ramiz Mujkic to you?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I read it and saw it on television because it was broadcast live on BN TV, or rather, it was shown again.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: So you read his entire statement on the basis of a television broadcast or are you referring to his oral evidence?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I'm interested in the events that relate to Ahatovici and the reactions that relate to Ahatovici, I have various statements at home from witnesses from the Muslim side, and that included Ramiz's statement. I know Ramiz very well, and I can tell you that he gave a quite fair statement but he didn't describe his side. He augmented the role of the Serbs and he got the dates a bit wrong. I don't quite agree with him as far as the dates are concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Did any member of the Defence team provide you with that statement?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I read it when they came to see me in my home.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Okay. So my question --

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. Those statements are old ones. I don't know when he previously testified. These statements go back to -- well, I don't know which years. Probably when he had been released, but I didn't read this statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: My question was: Did any member of the Defence team provide you with a statement of Ramiz Mujkic?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO [Resumed]
utterances.text: We went through this when we had a conversation with Mr. Karadzic, but I didn't read it --

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: It's a simple yes or no question. Did a member of the Defence team provide you with a statement of Ramiz Mujkic?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had a look at Ramiz Mujkic's statement during my conversation with the president. I had it in my hands and read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Did a member of the Defence team provide you with a statement of Ramiz Mujkic?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, have you understood what I said? I had the statement in my hands, and I read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's put it this way: Where did you get that statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I had my conversation with the president, that is when I read through that statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, when did you get that statement for the first time and from whom did you get that statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't remember. It was a long time ago. I read through some old statements, not only Ramiz Mujkic's statement. Someone would obtain the statement, then phone you up and say, We have a statement, let's see what the enemy side has to say. So I can't remember. It's not as if I only have Ramiz Mujkic's statement. I have the statements of other witnesses too because I am interested in Ahatovici and that is why I took care to read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could the Chamber move into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Back to you, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I want to move now to the motive for the establishment of Rajlovac municipality. Before I do, can we -- we've agreed that after the Serb take-over of Ahatovici, the entire Muslim population of Ahatovici was taken away; we agree on that, do we?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we do not. The Muslim population at the beginning of July was, or rather, it was in June, was either taken away or they left of their own will. As far as I can see here, Rajlovac municipality was set up sometime in February, up to the month of June, up to the 2nd of June, or rather, up to the 29th of May, 1992. The Serbs, the Muslims, and the Croats were equal and lived freely in Rajlovac municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: At page 2857 [sic] of yesterday's transcript you were giving an answer after I had asked you about the date of Muslim civilians from Ahatovici surrendering to Serb forces. You said that it started on the 31st of May and lasted until the 2nd of June. You went on to say, "Only the Ahatovici local commune which was inhabited by Muslims." That's how you were referring to Ahatovici, and later on you said: "As for the civilians from Ahatovici, more specifically the villages in Ahatovici which composed one-third of the local commune, they were indeed taken to Rajlovac." Do you recall that evidence?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember because you confused me with all those questions. I know very little. This is now a fair question. Thank you, Your Honours, for giving me a break. I'm much more stable today and my answers will be better today than yesterday. When it comes to the local commune of Dobrosevici, according to the 1991 census - and I had a relative there and I helped them with the census - there were 1.066 Muslims, 999 Serbs, I don't remember the number of Croats. I remember those two numbers because they were very characteristic. Moreover, the fighting started during the night between the 29th of May and the 30th of May, 1992, by the mortar attack on our positions, mounted by the Muslims. Probably from the 31st of May until the 2nd of June, the Muslim civilians surrendered in that local commune. On the 4th of June, when we entered Ahatovici, there was sporadic feeble fire. One Serbian soldier died and two Muslim soldiers died, but there were no civilians. In other words, until the 2nd of June, all the civilian population had been evacuated.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: When you say they had been evacuated, you mean they had been taken to the barracks at Rajlovac?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not a direct participant in all that so I can't tell you any facts. However, according to other people's words, the southern parts or the lower parts, excluding Ahatovici, had seen all the civilians surrender and some of them, as far as I know, were taken not to be exchanged. They expressed a wish to be taken to Sarajevo and they were escorted to the Croatian barricades in the village of Dobri [phoen]. When it comes to Ahatovici, that happened on the 2nd of June. Most probably all of those civilians ended up in Rajlovac. I'm talking about the 500 civilians, including women, children, and elderly. I cannot confirm this for a fact. I heard it from others and I believe that to be true.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And as you point out in paragraph 68 of your statement, in the Serbian municipality of Rajlovac there were three Muslims: Daughter, Bahra Pasic and her parents. That's at the bottom of paragraph 68. So can we agree after the Serb take-over of Ahatovici, the entire Muslim population of Ahatovici --

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know, I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: -- was removed?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some were removed, some left of their own will. I absolutely agree. However, yesterday when you put that question to me you did not understand my answer. It is absolutely true that in Bojnik or in that general local commune after the fighting, not only Bahra and her father and mother remained. A few more families were left behind. I can't tell you exactly how many people. But in any case, for example, the entire Pasic family that comprised several households, they were isolated because there had been problems with the barracks in Butile, they were isolated in some weekend cottages and they did not have the right to move around freely in the direction of their own houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yesterday at page 29852 you said in Rajlovac municipality only economic reasons were in place for Rajlovac municipality to separate from Novi Grad municipality. My question is: Is it your position that there was no ethnically based motive for the establishment of Rajlovac municipality?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would kindly ask the Trial Chamber to allow me to finish my previous answer because I believe that the Prosecutor did not understand me and I believe that the Trial Chamber would benefit from the rest of my answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If the microphone was on, immediately after the fighting, after the conflict, not just the three Muslims were left behind in Bojnik village. It's half of the local community. I don't know what happened in Bilokeci [phoen] and Dobrosevici because there were a lot more happenings there. The entire Pasic was left behind. Please do not hold me to the number. I believe that there were some 50 of them. As for the three people I mentioned, Bahra and her parents, they remained there through the war. One of them died and was buried in a regular fashion. The remainder of the Pasic family left of their own will towards Kiseljak -- I have no finished, please. Not only the Pasic family remained. There were also the Croatian family Bosnjak. On the one hand I had the Croatian family as my first neighbours and on the other side I had Muslims. The entire Bosnjak families remained there and lived there throughout the war. Younger members of that family, there was some who volunteered and joined the Serbian units and there were others who left without any problems because they didn't want to participate in the war. They left and now they live in Italy, Sweden, and God knows where. Sir, you confused me yesterday when you put that question to me and I did not provide you with the right answer and now I can do it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Dzino, it is not appropriate comment that the Prosecutor, Mr. Gaynor, confused you. I don't think he did. Could you try to answer the question about the reason for the separation or establishment of Rajlovac. Do you remember the question? Or shall I ask him to repeat that question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I remember. No problem there. I wouldn't be able to tell you exactly; however, Rajlovac municipality had existed up to the 1950s and Novi Grad municipality did not exist at the time. Novi Grad municipality was then set up and comprised a territory of Rajlovac municipality. It was an industrial area in that part of Novi Grad municipality. Since all the income, all the profit from those companies were sent to Novi Grad and very little was left for the municipality of Rajlovac, the main reason, the principal reason, was the economic reason. Because when you look at the map you will see that all of our roads were macadam roads, that they were dirt roads, and Mr. Ramiz Mujkic could confirm to you and say that we financed our own waterworks and telephone lines with very little financial aid from Novi Grad municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. Dzino, you refer at paragraph 14 of your statement to Jovo Bozic, who was the president of the Serb municipality of Rajlovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could I call up, please, 65 ter 17258.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. Dzino, you know Jovo Bozic, don't you?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Right. We're going to have a look at what he said about the motive for the establishment of Rajlovac municipality. Now, as you can see from the opening paragraph -- there is an English translation of this. As you can see from the opening paragraph this is a statement of Jovo Bozic. And in the first sentence it -- the statement is dated the 17th of the 12th, 1992. And the first sentence of the statement he says: "I was appointed president of the Serbian municipality of Rajlovac in the month of May and I am still upholding that position."

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: We'll try and get the English uploaded. There certainly is an English version available.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: First of all, can you confirm that in that opening paragraph he names the members of the war commission and one of those members is Mirko Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And can you confirm that in that paragraph he says that apart from those members of the war commission, the commander of Rajlovac brigade, the head of the public security service sector, and head of the police station Rajlovac were also present at the meetings on a regular basis, meetings of the war commission were held every day, and prior to that every three days. The war commission was responsible for global security situation in the area of the municipality and it was giving directions regarding certain matters. That's what it says there; correct? Have you read that, sir?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know when they met, in what composition. I believe at that time - and that was in the month of May -- is that so? I can't see it. Can you tell me when this document was issued?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: This document is dated the 17th of December, 1992. Now, it's true, isn't it, that Mirko Krajisnik --

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mirko, Mirko. I'm interested in the month of May. What is the date in the month of May when this was happening? Well, go on then. Put your question to me now.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: First of all, let's clarify, Mirko Krajisnik is the brother of Momcilo Krajisnik; right?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And I think that we can accept in the first paragraph of this statement the president of the municipality of Rajlovac is naming the members of the war commission and he is confirming that the war commission met with the head of the police station and the head of the public security service sector on a regular basis; do you agree?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. I'm not aware of that. I'm not -- I was not a member of that commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Right. Well, let's move to his description of the motive for the formation of the Serb municipality of Rajlovac. That's at the bottom of this page, please. Now, in the first words of that paragraph -- Their Honours do not have a copy of this statement in English so would you kindly start reading the last paragraph on this statement, sir? And could you read it into the record and we'll continue until the end of the paragraph?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Dzino, if you could read it aloud we can hear the interpretation. So could you read it aloud for the benefit of the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "The motive for the setting up of the Serbian municipality of Rajlovac was its existence up to the year 1958 when it was disbanded only because it was inhabited by a majority Serb population. In order to prevent an even bigger expansion in the settling of Muslims in the area which has increased as well as the legal building of houses, before the war a Serbian municipality of Rajlovac had been set up. All that was done with a view to preserving the Serbian territory and is closely connected with all the political circles which in the multi-party period of the government in the former Bosnia and Herzegovina represented the Serbian people and its interests in this area." Should I go on? Do you want me to go on reading?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Well, in fact, yes, the next portion concerns the person who whom Jovo Bozic reported to and some of the people he met. So if I can ask you to read the next --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it that now we have the English translation available?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we upload them together.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Well, first of all, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. I apologise, sir. Can this be blown up for me?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: That's all right. I'll ask you a question about the bit you've just read out. It's clear from what you've read that according to Jovo Bozic, the motive for the establishment of the Serb municipality of Rajlovac was on the one hand to prevent an even greater expansion of the Muslims settling into the area and on the other hand of preserving Serbian territory. And all this was done in close connection with the political circles that represented the Serbian people. That's his position, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Right. Now, let's move on to the people to whom he reported. If we look at the second paragraph, if we go to page 2 in English, please, if you look at the second paragraph in your version, we see that Mr. Bozic said that he reported to Momcilo Krajisnik, president of the Assembly of Republika Srpska, on a regular basis, either directly by telephone regarding the decisions adopted at the meetings of the war commission, achieved results, and a global security situation in the area of the municipality. You see that?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I do see it, but the letters are really small. I can't really read it and I really don't know what I'm supposed to say about that, but go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: We'll come to that. He later refers to meetings with the most responsible persons from the command of the armed forces in the Republika Srpska, General Ratko Mladic and Colonel Galic. Later on he confirms that General Sipcic and Colonel Galic, representatives of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, visited the municipality on a couple of occasions. And further down below we see that he says: "As president of the municipality I was in regular contact with the command personnel of Rajlovac brigade, especially with commander and chief of the staff." Now, I put it to you, Mr. Dzino, that the Serb take-over of Ahatovici was part of a plan co-ordinated at the highest levels to remove the Muslim population from Ahatovici and to remove the non-Serb population from the newly established municipality of Rajlovac.

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Was there a question for me anywhere?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, I'm putting that case to you. I'm putting that interpretation of the events to you. I'm inviting you to respond in any way you wish.

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that you're not right. In the entire city of Sarajevo and its surroundings, there was shooting in March. On the 22nd of April, there was an attack on Ilidza. I don't know about Vogosca. It was behind the hills. We could not communicate with them. However, we watched the fighting in Nedzarici and Ilidza with the naked eye. I attended meetings where we talked to Hasan Mujkic, I personally talked to him, and I was imploring with him not to start a war in our local commune. If he wanted to wage a war, he should go across the Bosnia where there was fighting going on. In other words, up to the 29th of May, 1992, up to 8.00 in the evening it was peaceful in our area. All the skirmishes that happened during the night, there were no wounded, there were no casualties, people were working on their land, and it was peaceful up to the 29th of May, 1992. In other words, nobody ever ordered me to take Ahatovici, nor were we actually capable of doing that. We simply defended ourselves in that area. I suppose that you will have other questions for me about that, then I will feel free to go into greater length about the situation on the 29th of May, but I can do it now if you wish. In any case, up to that time, up to then, it was peaceful. One more thing, I know Jovo Bojic [as interpreted], Mirko Krajisnik, and all those people you mentioned, I know who they are, but up to that time I had never seen them. I -- obviously I know Momcilo Krajisnik as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: We'll move on to another subject now, sir. At paragraph -- this concerns snipers. At paragraph 66 of your statement you say that you were a member of the Rajlovac Light Infantry Brigade. At paragraph 56 of your statement you say you never saw a professional sniper in your unit or other units of the SRK?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Very well. I'd like to show you a document and that is 65 ter 23827. Mr. Dzino, as you can see, this document is dated the 3rd of November, 1993, and it bears a stamp in the top left corner of the command of the Rajlovac Light Infantry Brigade. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: It appears to be addressed to the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps command?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 1 do you see that the commander states that due to an intense shortage of manpower in our brigade, we are, for the time being, unable to set up a unit as ordered, but instead have available two groups of snipers doing the work.

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO [Resumed]
utterances.text: And your question is?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Well, if we move down to paragraph 3 we see that he lists the equipment he has available, including nine pieces of an M76, 7.9-millimetre sniper rifle.

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Question?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Do you therefore accept that the Rajlovac Light Infantry Brigade did, in fact, have snipers and did have sniper rifles?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, according to establishment, every squad, every group of ten soldiers, should have that. And this is what the Light Infantry Brigade had, I'm reading: M76 sniper, nine pieces, probably belonging to the brigade; then five 56-millimetre sniper, one piece, privately owned; and M48 carbine, three pieces privately owned, which means that we're talking about hunting rifles. I suppose so. I don't know for a fact. I can't find this, but I know for a fact what I know for a fact. Probably in the paragraph that you have just quoted I told you that we did not have a professional sniper. I didn't see them. Do you know who those snipers were? They were just foot soldiers that had not been trained. They were carrying sniper rifles. They were better shooters than others. If there are any military experts here, they can tell you how long a sniper should be trained for, how they should behave to be effective. This is an order. I know who issued that order. I know who drafted it. I can see from the signature. There is no dispute about that. This is true. However, it says here due to a shortage of manpower they need snipers in order to protect their units. This is not about any military establishment. Those were people who were on the positions who were better shooters, therefore they were called snipers.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: So it's your evidence, is it, that the reference to nine M76, 7.9-millimetre sniper rifles in this document is, in fact, a reference to privately owned hunting rifles; is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no, you haven't understood me. Listen, it says 7.9 M76 sniper, nine pieces. I assumed that this was the property of the army. The following paragraph, 5.56 sniper, one piece, it says in brackets "privately owned," at least that's what it says in my document; 7.9 -millimetre carbine, three pieces, privately owned. So in the document -- this is a report, I assume, to SRK corps and they are informed that they have four privately owned snipers and nine military ones. We're dealing with a brigade. A brigade should have a hundred snipers, as per establishment roughly speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd like to tender that document, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that will be admitted as next Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P5976, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd like to take you now, please, to paragraph 29 of your statement, and you were referring to the hand-over of captives to soldiers from the Rajlovac Brigade. In that paragraph you say that one of the officers whose name you do not know gave you a brochure of the Geneva Conventions on warfare. You say: "I had not been acquainted with the content of the conventions from before, but once I read it I realised that we acted completely properly with captives and the dead members of the enemy army." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it's not a problem, could you tell me which paragraph it is in?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Paragraph 29.

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: All right. I'd like you to tell us a little bit more about the circumstances of this incident. How big was this brochure of the Geneva Conventions on warfare?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a brochure that I received at that time from the officer whose name I can't remember. He was a Macedonian, Apostolovski, something like that, I don't know exactly. I wouldn't like to speculate about his name. I did my military service in the JNA in 1971 and 1972. At a course I was informed of the Geneva Conventions. I had never previously read all of the conventions. Throughout the war I was concerned about doing something bad, something that might happen to my people too. I read the Geneva Conventions and we did everything we could to abide by the Geneva Conventions. But as for the fighting, people who were killed in combat, well that was a military matter. These are the Geneva Conventions that I had brought with me. I mentioned them in the statement and I kept these conventions with me throughout the war time period.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the transcript, if I may. It doesn't say that the witness said as far as combat is concerned, if they weren't dead, I and my people would be dead. That was not recorded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Karadzic. Mr. Dzino, could you speak a little bit slower for the benefit of the Chamber to hear you -- hear you out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll try.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: So once Apostolovski gave you this brochure, did you sit yourself down immediately and read the entire brochure until you were satisfied that you had acted scrupulously in accordance with it?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Chamber will caution me again, but at that time there was fighting. A man gave me a brochure, said be careful, respect the Geneva Conventions, et cetera. So there was fighting. I had to sit down and read the conventions, the Geneva Conventions. I read the Geneva Conventions on the first day I was free, but up until that point in time there was continuous fighting. I don't want to be warned by the Chamber, cautioned by the Chamber, but really don't ask me such questions. When there is fighting then you are concerned with beating the enemy and remaining alive. You don't spend time reading conventions.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: The incidents you're describing happened shortly after the take-over of Ahatovici by Serb forces, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which incidents? Which incidents are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: The incident when Apostolovski gave you a copy of the brochure of the Geneva Conventions.

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. This was on the 2nd of June, 1992. Can I describe the event?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my unit, in my area of the zone of responsibility, the Serbs didn't enter Ahatovici up until the 2nd of June, 1992. An old man born in 1939 Mladjen Lemez disappeared. I ordered my soldiers not to let him go because he had a house and stables and two cows there in sort of no man's land. The next day they said Mladjen wasn't there. Mladjen went to feed the livestock and then he disappeared. When they told me about this, I and three other soldiers went to look. I went to that no-man zone. I approached the house. I saw Mladjen Lemez on the metal railings, against the metal railings. He was dead. I can't say now whether half his head had been blown off or cut off. The corpse had been there for a while because there were maggots in it. We entered the house and the stables. We had a look around. We assumed that there were enemy soldiers there. At that point in time as that is the terrain, there is a sort of hill and there was a stream above us and we noticed a group of soldiers. In the statement I said that there were 50 of them. It wouldn't be a large number for you, but there were far more of them. As our position was unfavourable, we had to take action. They were in a column, advancing in a column. At the head of the column there was Hasan Mujkic. They were so near that I could recognise the first few men. They were all in camouflage uniforms and were wearing helmets and they were all armed. The four of us took up our positions, opened fire, threw grenades at them, and that group of soldiers went back. In the meantime, as the fighting broke out, let me point out that we did not have any communication with the unit. We didn't have any Motorolas. There was only a courier connection. I informed the unit of the positions to come and assist us. In the meantime the Muslims had regrouped and attacked the Serbian houses in Petrovici to the right of us. The unit had already been informed that they had been attacked. They were caught in cross-fire and 13 men were killed and 19 taken captive. And allow me to finish. Of those 13 men who were killed, neighbours of mine on the whole, a few of them were neighbours. Of the 13 killed men I only knew two of them. And I -- I was born in 1951. I was 42 at the time. I went to work with those men, I knew them. There were ten men whom I didn't know. Of the 19 captives, there were only a few whom I knew. All the others were from elsewhere. And let me finish. A while ago you mentioned nine snipers in the Rajlovac Brigade. When we gathered the weapons from those who had been killed and wounded, well there was an Osa hand-held rockets-launcher, there were ten Zoljas, there were seven snipers. In my statement there is a printing error, there were five military snipers and there were two, I don't know, American weapons, that's what we call them. I apologise. Let me finish. They had special handmade knives for slaughtering. They had tools to take out people's eyes. So this was the so-called nice army and we were bad guys and my Rajlovac Brigade at that time, I don't know the date, had a total of nine snipers. Are you satisfied with that? I haven't finished yet, so --

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. Dzino, you -- could you just focus on the questions which are put to you and answer those questions. The -- it was on the 2nd of June, 1992, that Apostolovski gave you a copy of the brochure. You read it carefully and you satisfied yourself that you were acting in accordance with the Geneva Conventions; correct? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Okay. This was -- could we call up, please, P4070 e-court, page 202. Two days after this, the mosque at Ahatovici was blown up, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: We'll just confirm the damage to that mosque in a moment. Those are photographs taken in 1996 of what once was the Ahatovici mosque; isn't that right, Mr. Dzino?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume so.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, does that appear to you to be consistent with a rigid application of the Geneva Conventions?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have to provide a detailed answer. I'm testifying here on my own behalf. I am defending my actions and the actions of my unit. My unit wasn't in Ahatovici taking the mosque there. I'm not aware of that. At the beginning of the -- my testimony, I suggested that you show a map of our local commune. Everything would be clear to you in such a case. Now you're asking me this question. My unit was only on one side of Ahatovici; other units were on the other side. We didn't have any contact. I don't know what was going on on the other side. I'm talking about a platoon. I would like us to have a map of the area that I defended. This wasn't in the area of my responsibility. I saw this from a distance of about 1 kilometre, and I am testifying that it was blown up. I saw the explosion. As for how it happened, well -- the Geneva Conventions, I had the Geneva Conventions in my pocket and I abided by them. If others didn't, that's not my problem. Now you asked me about the military and how the Rajlovac municipality was established. I couldn't be the commander of the platoon and the president of the Rajlovac municipality or the Crisis Staff at the time -- at the same time. So you should ask me questions only if I can answer these questions. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: No further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Karadzic, do you have re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Excellencies. There are a few matters that I have to clarify that arose in the course of the cross-examination. Good morning, Your Excellencies. Good morning to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Lieutenant, sir, on page 29 in the question it was suggested that the mosque was blown up. You were asked to confirm that and you said "yes." And then this photograph was shown. Did we have a shell as part of our weapons that had a charge that could dispel parts of the mosque a hundred metres away?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO [Resumed]
utterances.text: My unit had automatic weapons. It didn't have shells of any kind, or rather, we had a hand-held rocket-launcher.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could a hand-held rocket-launcher cause such damage to the mosque?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would have found that incredible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were asked about the Serbian municipality of Rajlovac. Could we very briefly have a look at P2329. I apologise. That's a mistake. It's probably -- just bear with me a minute. Do you recognise this signature? There is no stamp, but do you recognise the signature?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you agree that there is no protocol and no stamp on the document and the signature is not a familiar one?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's quite correct. I can't recognise the signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you aware of the fact that the municipality was also responsible for defending its own territory within the Territorial Defence and the president of the municipality was the president of the defence council as well?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if it didn't have such responsibility, the municipality and the president of the municipality, if that hadn't been the case we would have organised ourselves and defended ourselves, because that was the situation. The president was only performing his duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now I would like to have a look at the document on the promulgation of a law -- but before we find it could we see 1D3259. You were asked about the late Jovo Bozic, the president of the Municipal Assembly of Rajlovac?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We don't have a translation. We weren't going to tender this. You weren't asked about the circumstances. Could I ask you to have a look at the last paragraph in the first column. Since it's very small, I'll read it out. In the answer it says: "Through the will of communist prominent people and as part of the new territorial organisation, the municipality in Rajlovac in 1959 was disbanded. It was a matter of breaking up the Serbian corps in the area. In 1974 when the Novo Sarajevo municipality became too large, initiative was taken to establish another municipality. It would be logical for that municipality to be," and then we go on to the next page. "It would be logical to renew the work of the municipality of Rajlovac, but there were two other suggestions that were deliberately made and they concern Sarajevsko Polje and Novi Grad. Without having consulted the people it was decided through an election that the new municipality should be called Novi Grad Sarajevo. So they were out-voted." So does this tally with the information that you have about the fate of the municipality of Rajlovac? You could answer this question by simply saying yes or no.

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's see what it says further down in the column on the second page. I'll read slowly: "It was only after the first multi-party elections in the former Bosnia and Herzegovina that there was an opportunity to find a remedy to this injustice. We created a committee for establishing the municipality. And in a plebiscite of the Serbian people on remaining in Yugoslavia we made a suggestion to the people and asked them to say how to divide the territory" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The accused is kindly asked to slow down when reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "... the answer was a hundred per cent positive." Let me ask you the following: Do you remember that before the war for economic, cultural, and other reasons there was an action that was carried out in many large municipalities in order to establish a number of municipalities, the Serbian municipality of Rajlovac, the Muslim municipality of Rajlovac, the Serbian municipality of Novo Sarajevo, and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in fact all the people wanted to be compact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we go back to the first page. In the second paragraph we have the answer. I'll read this out slowly: "From individual Muslims and other sources, we had precise information on the semi-illegal work of the SDA. Just before the war broke out they started distributing weapons openly. The centre where extremists gathered were mosques in Sokolje and Brijesce Brdo where Alija Izetbegovic and Muhamed Cengic often went. The Muslims were so arrogant that at public meetings they openly started threatening the Serbs. Later we obtained certain names and lists of members of the SDA to whom the party promised up to 1.500 square metres of Serbian land when the Chetniks were driven out." Does this also agree or tally with the information that you had at that time?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely, but one should also add the mosque in Ahatovici to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Objection. That's one of the clearest examples of a leading questions that I've seen so far. Indeed, Mr. Karadzic said, "In the second paragraph we have the answer." This again -- once again he has openly defied the Trial Chamber's instructions to refrain from asking leading questions in re-examination. We've seen that he does know how to ask non-leading questions. I would request him to ask non-leading question in redirect examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you tell us again why this is a leading question?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: First of all, he says, "In the second paragraph we have the answer." He reads it out. And then he says, "Does this agree or tally with the information that you have at that time." This is coming on the back of a couple of questions earlier on where he's essentially leading the witness in the direction that he wants the witness to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I tend to agree with you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I respond? My question was whether this tallied with his information. As for everything else, I was reading out an interview. These weren't my questions. I read out what Bozic himself said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The rule is simply this, Mr. Karadzic, you are suggesting the answer by the way you are putting your question; that's why it's a leading question. Please keep that in mind.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellencies. I'll just adhere to the text. I can ask him what he knows about this because Bozic became part of this testimony because of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, my question is: How does this tally with what you knew?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't know what was happening in Brijesce Brdo and Sokolje; however, there was a similar situation in Ahatovici. Prominent functionaries from the SDA, from Ahatovici, like Izetbegovic, Bakir Izetbegovic, he later became the MUP minister; there were regular visits to his house without any problems. But he would bring in Cengic, for example, Pusin. It was said that Alija Izetbegovic also went there. So there were frequent visits of high-level functionaries from the SDA to Ahatovici during that period of time. There was a similar situation, or rather, after Ahatovici had been taken we saw that they were very well armed, well organised, and you didn't give me the opportunity to provide you with more assistance because they had 262 soldiers from local inhabitants who were in 11 platoons. So the organisation was a military one. Positions had been fortified with trenches, et cetera, whereas in our case people didn't want to dig. They were behind their houses, behind trees, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could I draw your attention to another paragraph which I will read out very slowly. It's to the right of this one: "The first real fighting started on Zuc, or rather, on the slopes above the Zrak company. On the 8th of June, the Muslims carried out a terrible crime there. They set fire to 25 Serbian houses. And entire families Pajdakovici [phoen], Breza, Simonici [phoen], Starcevici, Babici, Odzakovici, and others saved themselves by fleeing to the headquarters of the municipality." How does this tally with your information, the information that you had?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. In fact, my family is also concerned here. I saw those people, I listened to their stories, that they were slaughtered, massacred.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we go to the following page. It says here in the second line: "This is the real truth and not what General Kukanjac is saying. He did not help us at all with anything. On the contrary, his subordinate officer Miletic, the then-commander of the Rajlovac barracks, distributed 247 automatic rifles to Muslims in Sokolje and Brijesce Brdo as well as combat kits." Was this Miletic a Serb, judging by his family name?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, judging by his family name I suppose so, so probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about that? Do you know that the JNA behaved objectively, as they say, and distributed weapons among the Muslim?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in connection with your specific question. I can tell you that we knew that the arms were distributed among Serbs and Muslims, but I -- let me tell you about an event. I came across a neighbour, a Muslim, in 1998. And since we had been good friends, he told me jokingly, I know when you received automatic rifles, but so that you know we got machine-guns, which means that they fared better than us.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, is the transcript enough or should we tender this interview into evidence to be marked for identification while the translation is pending? I know that it's very hard to admit second-hand interviews, but in this case maybe what has entered into the transcript will suffice. Maybe the Trial Chamber will rely only on that and will not need to admit the document as such.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I tend to agree with that suggestion, in particular given his statement in the military court was not tendered. Do you have further re-examination, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, a few more questions and I will need about 20 more minutes or perhaps 15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then that being the case, we'll take a break now. We'll break for half an hour and resume at three past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And now I would like to call up 65 ter 17258. We have already seen that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting, Lieutenant, sir, was your unit geared towards an urban part and where was its contact point with the enemy?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, President, can you refer me to a specific period?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Objection, Mr. President. I don't recall this arises out of the cross-examination. This could have been raised in direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. How does it arise from the cross-examination of Mr. Gaynor?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Lieutenant told us that by establishment they were supposed to have a hundred snipers. I'm interested in their use. How come a brigade should have a hundred snipers? What would be their role?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So is that a question for the witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Okay. Let's do it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What would that many sniper rifles do in a brigade? What would they be used for?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not answer in that sense. I did not say that my brigade should have had a hundred sniper rifles. I was comparing it to a platoon which had seven sniper rifles. Following that logic, a brigade should have a hundred sniper rifles. We didn't. We had that one platoon and at the beginning of the war on the 2nd of June is what we had, and I answered the question in that sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In other words, your brigade had less than one Muslim platoon?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that particular platoon.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at page 7 in both languages, page 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is an interview by the late Mr. Bozic. I'm going to read the second paragraph where he says: "According to the information I have due to sniping activities by the enemy in the barracks, about 40 people were killed and about 100 wounded. In relation to this I asked Colonel Galic from the corps to undertake energetic measures in order to neutralise snipers. As far as I know, he ordered Lieutenant-Colonel Golijanin to burn down the bushes which the enemy used for their snipers, but the command of the Rajlovac Brigade failed to do anything in this respect. "Likewise, the brigade command allowed enemy snipers to sneak into the settlement of Bacici and also enemy is digging bunkers in the embankment area towards Brijesce in failing to undertake any measures to prevent those things." How does this tally with what you know?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The fact is that most of the soldiers were killed by sniping and the reason was the fact that we were in a subordinated position, in a less-favourable position. We were in a field when the Muslims were up in the hills. In front of us we had the Sokolje settlement which, according to some rough estimates, had about 1500 houses, which means that from each window, from each roof-top, sniper fire could be opened. We were literally in a meadow before we could dig ourselves in and fortify our positions. Before that, a lot of our soldiers died due to sniping incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before we proceed further. Mr. Gaynor, since this was not tendered can I ask you in what context Mr. Bozic gave this statement in the military court? Can you assist us?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'm not entirely sure about that from the content of the statement itself. It appears to relate to the activities of paramilitary groups that -- and he was questioned about that, including Brne Gavrilovic. If Your Honours wish to admit this statement, I have no objection. If Mr. Karadzic wants to tender it, I’ve no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's see how it evolves. Thank you, Mr. Gaynor. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You therefore are telling us about soldiers being killed by sniper fire. If your brigade had had sniper rifles, how would it have used it? Did it have an opportunity to open fire on the city?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our brigade did not need sniper rifles. We had no targets for sniper rifles. We were in an unfavourable position so we couldn't target anything. As far as the city is concerned, the city could not be targeted. It could be targeted by artillery weapons, but when it comes to sniper rifle we did not even see the city. From our positions, it was impossible to see the city, let alone anything else. And moreover, when Brijesce Polje is mentioned, in front of us we had an embankment, a railway track, some high-rise building; for example, Centrotrans and others. On the right side we had the Valter Peric company, and so on and so forth. I can't remember all of those buildings. If I had a map I could tell you more. Therefore, we actually didn't need sniper rifles. The line was so close to us that we could open fire from ordinary infantry weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I will try to put questions to which you will be able to answer yes or no. The buildings that you have just mentioned, were they residential or commercial buildings?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were commercial buildings.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go to the following page, page 8. I'm interested in just one more paragraph in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the middle I'm going to read a couple of sentences: "Immediately before the war, contacts were established with the Muslim staffs around Rajlovac in order to strike a mutual agreement on refraining from mutual attacks. On such occasions, delegations were set up, so once I was sent Ahatovici. I also know that Radoljub Bato Milicevic was a member of a delegation that went to Boljakov Potok, and so on and so forth. How does this tally with what you know?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know when the late Jovo Bozic went to Ahatovici. I really don't know. I know that in my local commune meetings were organised, that they were initiated by the Serbs, and subject was refraining from attacks, good neighbourly relations, and so on and so forth. There were many such attacks, even on the eve of the start of the fighting. Hasan Mujkic came to one of those meetings. He was armed. He was wearing a camouflage uniform. He bore the markings of the Skorpions and Green Berets. He had two escorts. He gave us some conditions which we did not accept, and then he left the meeting, followed by all the Muslims because he had ordered them to leave the meeting.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now see P2315.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you were asked why the Serbian municipality of Rajlovac had been set up and you answered that you believed it was not the Serbian municipality of Rajlovac that was originally set up, but just the municipality of Rajlovac. In the former municipality of Rajlovac, were Ahatovici, Dobrosevici, and Zabrdje and all those settlements part of that municipality?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please slow down.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this part here be zoomed in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you both -- both of you slow down in putting the question and answering the question. Do you understand that, sir, Mr. Dzino? Please put -- yeah, please put a pause before --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- you start answering the question. Yes, please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I don't know how much you know about legal matters, Lieutenant. However, I want to ask you a question which will not be leading. Is this a decree on the promulgation of the law or some other decision, the thing that I signed here?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a decree.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this municipality being set up as a Serbian municipality of Rajlovac or just the municipality of Rajlovac?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just the municipality of Rajlovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We don't need this document anymore. In other words, a law is one thing and the promulgation of such a law is a different thing?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We mentioned Mr. Mujkic here. He testified in this case on 25th February on page 12436. He said that they did not have any trenches or bunkers, that they did not have that and that he didn't remember that he had ever said that -- I suppose that he was confronted with his previous statement. He said that he didn't -- they didn't have mortars or howitzers. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The complete village of Ahatovici was surrounded by bunkers, trenches. On the 2nd of June, when we stormed the first bunkers, we found field telephones connected with wire lines. We didn't even know what those were. In my previous statement, I didn't mention that one 60-millimetre mortar was taken from that group. I did not finish. In the night between 29 and 30 May, fire was opened at us from 82-millimetre mortars. I was there and I knew that it was the case because I saw the launchers that remained in the ground. I knew that those were 82-millimetre mortars.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Lieutenant, sir. I have no further questions for you. Thank you for having come here to testify.

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Unless my colleagues have questions for you, that concludes your evidence, Mr. Dzino. On behalf of the Chamber, I would like to thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. Now you are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have a request, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I say good-bye to the President? We celebrate the same religious holiday.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I tender a copy of the Geneva Conventions if Mr. Dzino doesn't want to part with the original?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is it necessary? Do we not have the Geneva Convention already? We saw it, it was recorded, and I think it's not necessary to tender it. But if you insist I will discuss it with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to demonstrate how it looked, what the document looked like when it was distributed at the beginning of the war. I'm not interested in the contents, but the form.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I think Mr. Karadzic is referring to the brochure, not the entirety of the conventions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: -- and its appendices, but we have no objection if a copy is made of this witness's copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Then the Registry will get a photocopy of that brochure with the assistance of Mr. Dzino. Thank you. Please have a safe journey back home. You said that already. It has been conveyed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, no, no, that's sufficient. You said that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And who is our next witness, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Predrag Trapara.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Let's bring him in. Let us give the exhibit number for the brochure.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit D2388, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could take the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please take a seat and make yourself comfortable. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Trapara.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to call up 1D6082 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Trapara, did you provide my Defence with a statement and do you see it now in front of you on the screen?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you read it? Does it accurately reflect what you had to say?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes, I read it and it does reflect what I wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you sign the statement?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes, I signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
