utterances.text: I have to wait and I need to ask you to wait between questions and answers to allow the interpreters to interpret correctly. If I were to put the same questions to you, would your answers be the same?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes, they would be.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, I would like to tender this statement pursuant to 92 ter Rule with two additional documents in the package.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, could you clarify whether -- whether or not you're tendering his transcript of testimony in the Milosevic case?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, we're not, Mr. President. This statement was submitted before our discussion about this issue with the earlier witness. So it's the same position. We don't tender it. But it was mentioned in the witness's statement, and we'll try to avoid that happening in the future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So you're tendering only the map?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Gaynor, any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The statement and the associated exhibit, which is a map marked by the witness, will be tender -- will be admitted. Shall we give the number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, 65 ter 1D06082 will be Exhibit D2389 and 65 ter number 1D08535 will be Exhibit D2390.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I'm going to read a short summary of Mr. Trapara's statement in English. [In English] Predrag Trapara lived in Lukavica. He was commander of the 5th Company of the 2nd Infantry Battalion of the 1st Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade. In September 1991 he used to see Juka Prazina with his armed paramilitary group at Mojmilo Brdo, where they conducted some sort of patrols. In contact with his company was the 2nd Battalion of the 101st Mountain Brigade of the 1st Corps of BH army. They had 82-millimetre-calibre mortars in the sector of Aneks. During the war, his unit engaged predominantly in defensive actions. The line of disengagement itself was created spontaneously because the Serbs went outside their own houses and the Muslims outside their own. This company never pushed the line of disengagement towards -- forward towards the Muslim territory nor did the opposed Muslim forces manage to move our -- Serb lines backwards. The units of the Muslim army ranged against them were much more numerous than his unit. They had infantry weapons, mortars, Brownings, heavy weapons, and an enormous number of sharpshooters. The latter were their strongest point. Serbian positions and civilians were exposed to sniper fire almost every day, and during the night Predrag Trapara's unit had to rig up shelters made of boards and blankets especially on the Lukavica-Pale road. Predrag Trapara and his unit had information and the data that civilian facilities were being used -- abused for military purposes by the opposing unit, information that he got from people who had fled from Muslim territory into the Serbian. This unit did not open fire at all on the depth of the enemy territory but on trenches on the line of disengagement. Muslim positions were often in the houses and cellars of houses which were on the line of confrontation, but there were no civilians in those houses according to his information. Never he, or any other member of his unit, or their subordinated or superior commands, intended to cause civilian casualties or terrorise civilians in the territory under Muslim control or exert psychological influence on them. They never received or issued any verbal or written orders to that effect. On the contrary, orders and instructions from superior commands were to open fire exclusively at the enemy army. The battalion commander -- command issued orders to his unit to the effect that civilians in the city section under the control of the Muslim authorities must not be the object of attack. With regard to water-supply, the battalion command ordered that Muslim settlements must be supplied with water. Civilians in the zone of responsibility of his unit were terrified as the shelling from the Muslim side was frequent. Civilian casualties and material damage to the civilian houses were usually within his zone of responsibility -- usual within his zone of responsibility. In February 1994, his mother was wounded in front of their house. She was wounded from a rifle and both her bones beneath the knees were broken and she is using crutches to this very day. Members of his unit were local people, inhabitants of that settlement, and he assesses their training level as medium. They had no trained professional sharpshooters. The command of the unit was composed by non-professional officers. This fact to a certain degree influenced the quality of direction, command and control of his unit. With regard to the ammunition stocks, they had no artillery. And as regards infantry ammunition, the situation tended to change. The permanent orders from superior commands to the expenditure of the ammunition were that ammunition must be used sparingly. His unit always let humanitarian relief pass through their territory. There were examples of abuse of humanitarian relief on the part of international forces. On one occasion the military police discovered seven rifles in the humanitarian supply intended for the Muslim part of the city. Muslim units ranged against them frequently violated cease-fires, and intensified works and digging of communication trenches towards Serb positions, work usually done under coercion by Serb civilians who had remained in the Muslim part of the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I only have one question as part of the examination-in-chief. Mr. Trapara, just prior to the war were you involved in an incident? Was there a misunderstanding that you had with the police? And if that's the case, could you tell the Chamber about the nature of that incident?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes, I did. In October 1991 there was an incident I was involved in that had to do with weapons. What do I mean by that? This is related to what was stated at the beginning of my statement; namely, that in September 1991 on Mojmilo hill just above my house I observed Juka Prazina with his paramilitary formation whose patrols and sporadic shooting caused unrest amongst the Serbian people in our territory. And the second half of October, my uncle woke me up at half past 1.00 in the morning. He told me to accompany him to the village of Miljevici. We also took a relative of mine with us. When we arrived up there, he parked his lorry. We didn't load anything onto the lorry. I didn't even know what we were to load. Later we set off in the direction of the village of Ivanic and that is where we located that lorry. Later it turned out that there were weapons in the lorry. Immediately, five minutes, after the lorry had come to a halt, a police patrol vehicle arrived with three policemen in it. I knew all three of them: One of them was Jure, a sergeant in Vrapce; the other one was Sulejman Zolj from Bistrik; and the third one was Pajdakovic [phoen] of Serbian ethnicity. That was up in the direction of Zuc or from the -- he was from the direction of Zuc. One of them only said, Who is the driver of this lorry? My uncle said, I am. Please get into the lorry. Sulejman, the policeman, got into the lorry with him. The two others, the two other policemen, entered the vehicle, or rather, the police patrol vehicle and escorted the lorry towards the Vrace sector and probably they later took them to the central prison. As far as we were concerned, I read the document that arrived from the MUP of the former SR of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and in that document it states that I and my relative fled, which is not true. On the following day, in the morning, I went to work as usual. I worked in post office number 2 in Sarajevo at the new station. I worked there for seven days. I didn't have any problems. And then two military policemen arrived in a patrol vehicle and informed me and my relative, who also worked in the post office with me, that we should go to the Viktor Bubanj barracks with them in order to give a statement there. We went there and we spent 29 days there. We were accused. There was a military court that put us on trial. After that period of time had elapsed, we were released, having been given a conditional sentence, and I returned to my usual work. I continued working in post office number 2 until the 3rd of April, 1992. And after that date I didn't return there because of my own safety.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Which army are we dealing with? Whose military policemen and which military court are we dealing? Who was prosecuting you?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: This was the army, or rather, the military policemen of the former JNA, two policemen from a former JNA. And the court in the Viktor Bubanj barracks was a military court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It was also a JNA court?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes, it was also a JNA court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no other questions for the moment so I give the floor to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Trapara, as you have noted, your evidence in chief was admitted in writing in lieu of your oral testimony. You will be now further cross-examined by the Prosecution. Yes, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Trapara.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: The witness statement that you've just confirmed, could you tell us which members of the Defence team took that statement from you?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Mr. Sladojevic, Marko.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Anybody else?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Was Milomir Savcic or Slobodan Batinic involved in the taking of your statement?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Well, before Mr. Marko, I first had contact with Milomir Savcic. Yes, that is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Did he take the first version of your statement from you?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't say that he took the first version.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: In any event, he was involved in preparing your statement, was he?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Have you ever been a member of a political party?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Which one?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: The SDS, the Serbian Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: When did you join it?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: I joined it after the Dayton Agreement, so that was around April 1996. I was on the list of deputies, but the elections were postponed for two years. So officially, the election was in 1998 but I was a party of the -- I was a member of the political party as of 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Are you still a member?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Well, in my heart but not actively.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd now like to turn to -- I'd like to confirm, first of all, that you did -- you were on the list of candidates for election in 1996, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And that was in the Municipal Assembly of Srpsko Novo Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: You also stood for election in 2005, and that was for the Municipal Assembly of Lukavica?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes, because by a decision from Serbian -- Serbian Novo Sarajevo couldn't have that name, so Lukavica was involved but it means the same thing. Because later it became eastern Sarajevo, so Lukavica was only a sort of transitional name.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And in both of those elections you did stand as a candidate of the Serb Democratic Party, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: I was a candidate in 1998, in the year 2000, and in the year 2004. And on all three occasions, I was elected as a national deputy. I had three mandates as a deputy from this political party.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: You did also stand in 1996 as well, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes. As I said, in 1996 I was a candidate and I became a member of the party at the time. However, the local elections were postponed and held two years later. So they didn't take place at the same time as the general election. So they took place after the general election. They would have been held in 1996, but they were postponed and held two years later.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd now like to turn to the incident on the 15th of October, 1991, when you were arrested for the illegal possession of weapons and explosives. Can you give the Court an idea of how many weapons were in the truck when the truck was stopped?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly. I know more or less what sort of weapons were in the truck, but I can't remember exactly what the quantity was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could you describe the kinds of weapons, please?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: There were these old weapons, so-called Dobosar 7.62-millimetre pistols and PAPs which are semi-automatic rifles, P-A-Ps.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Did you have any equipment -- excuse me, any ammunition in the truck?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes, I think there was some ammunition. It all took place so fast. The patrol arrived immediately. We had no time to do anything. Later we tried to guess what there was. We hadn't time to have a look inside, but I assumed there were these PAPs and these 7.62 -millimetre weapons, the so-called Dobosar weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Just give me an estimate of how many bullets were in that truck?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: I can't tell you exactly because I don't even know how many cases there were, let alone the number of rounds. I couldn't give you a precise number.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, do you accept the police record of this incident suggests that in that truck the police found two mortars; four boxes with four semi-automatic weapons; seven semi-automatic guns; four wooden boxes with 3.600, 7.9-millimetre bullets; eight boxes with 8.962 -- correction 8.960, 7.62-millimetre bullets; as well as two M53 machine-guns; other technical documentation relating to that stash; and cleaning equipment. Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Well, I accept it, but not the mortars. You understand, they took that away. We didn't have time to see exactly what there was. I accept all that. But I didn't hear anything about there being mortars amongst the weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: You were in the -- you were in that truck with Ignjatije Trapara; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: In the truck when it was stopped, you were with Ignjatije Trapara?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: He was taken away for questioning; right?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: As a result of that questioning, a further search was taken out -- was carried out at a place called the Aleksapromet company; correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: I don't know anything about Aleksapromet. I'm not familiar with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could we call up, please, 1D08653.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: At the top of this document you can see this is from the Ministry of Internal Affairs from the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and it is a bulletin of daily events for the 16th of October, 1991. If we go to the next page -- you agree with that, Mr. Trapara?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes, it's a bulletin and I do agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: If we go to the next page can we see a description of the incident. If we go to the next page in English the quantities of ammunition found in the truck are described in detail. And it goes on to relate that: "After the questioning of Ignjatije Trapara, a further search was taken out at -- took place at the Aleksapromet company ..." That's now visible on the English language. Do you see the relevant paragraph in the original? It's about halfway down that page, Mr. Trapara.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: I see it says PP Aleksapromet. I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: At that location the employees of CSB, SUP Sarajevo, and SJB Novo Sarajevo found eight boxes with ten semi-automatic guns; one box with nine semi-automatic guns; one box with two machine guns. Skip on a bit, we see reference to a box with three mortars; three cleaners; three optical aims; seven boxes with four mines; 22 boxes with 24.600, 7.62-millimetre bullets. You see all that?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: I can see that here.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Later on there's a reference to a further search which was carried out on a different truck. This is on the next -- this is on the same page in English. And we see that in the search of that truck the police found 78.400, 7.62-millimetre bullets and 77.425, 7.9 -millimetre bullets. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And I think you'll agree that these are vast quantities of weapons and ammunition to be transported around Sarajevo illegally. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Well, I didn't have this information. This is the first time I've come across this. I don't know whether this was all included. I couldn't see that night. I didn't load it. I didn't approach the lorry. Aleksapromet, this is something knew for me. There was some sort of Pilicari, but as for this information about the weapons and the ammunition, well, I really didn't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Are you related to Ignjatije Trapara?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: What is your relationship to him?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: He's my uncle.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, why were you assisting him in transporting large quantities of weapons and ammunition in Sarajevo on the 15th of October, 1991?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: He asked me, I went up there. Quite simply, I wanted to do this. The situation was such that our people were afraid. As I said earlier on, we had to organise ourselves. I went up there to see if I could protect myself and protect my family because this was at stake, not only in that area but in the Federation and in the wider area of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: First of all, let's clarify a couple of points in your answer. When you say that "our people were afraid," you're talking about the Serb people?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes. In this area of responsibility that I have shown in the map, 95 per cent of the people were of Serbian ethnicity and across the road from where we were there was the same percentage of Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, these weapons and ammunition were intended for distribution to the people of the Serb ethnicity; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Well, probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Well "probably" or "yes"? Was there any other reason for that?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't say yes, but probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And just clarify one other thing. You referred to the Federation in your answer. Given that this was 1991, was that an error on your part?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes, probably. Yes, I made a mistake. There was no Federation at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd like to tender that document, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P5977, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd like to turn now to the question of snipers. In your statement at paragraph 16 you say: "In my unit there were no trained professional sharpshooters." You were in the 1st Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, do you accept that within the 1st Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade there were considerable quantities of sniper weapons and optical equipment and silencers for sniper rifles? I'm not referring to a document which is on the screen at the moment. I'm simply asking you: Do you accept that contention?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could I call up, please, P05930.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be provided with a hard copy of his statement in Serbian?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have that with you, Mr. Trapara?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean the document, this one on the screen? What --

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Do you have a copy of your statement with you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Your statement, would you like to have that in hard copy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have the statement, I do. I have the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: You can turn to paragraph 16 if you wish. In any event, Mr. Trapara, on the screen in front of you we can see a document from the 1st Smbr to the SRK command. Do you see it?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: If -- as you can see in this document, the 1st Smbr is informing the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps that it's in possession of rifles with optical sights, semi-automatic rifles with optical sights, machine-guns with optical sights, other sniper rifles, passive infrared sights, sniper rifle silencers, and do you see all that?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: So you accept that your brigade did have at the time of this document all that equipment?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: What I stated just a while ago that I did not agree. I said that because I was not aware of that. I'm talking about my infantry company, mine, and my neighbourhood --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please slow down. It is impossible to interpret accurately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Trapara, you're speaking so fast that the interpreters are having difficulty --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you repeat your answer, previous answer, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I stated a while ago that I didn't agree with the Prosecutor, I did not have that document in front of me. I was only sharing the information that I had about my infantry company and the company next to mine. I'm sure that we did not have this type of weaponry.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, you see after the list of sniper rifles, et cetera, the brigade command is telling the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps command: "As we don't have a special sniper unit, we have issued the sniper rifles to combatants in the subordinated units. "They are active when the combatants are in position." So you accept that the brigade command issued sniper rifles to its subordinated units and that those subordinated units used them?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: That's what it says here in this document, but I didn't know about that. I was not aware of that. Possibly that was the case because my unit was on a slope of the Manojlo hilltop and we did not need any of those.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, I want to turn to a separate issue. At paragraph 17 of your statement in the first sentence, you say: "Humanitarian relief to the Muslim part of the city passed through my zone of responsibility. My unit always let such humanitarian relief pass through." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, you issued orders to your unit; is that right? You can put down your statement. This is a separate matter. Did your unit always obey your orders?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: As far as I know, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Did you receive your instructions from the brigade command?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: I did not receive any order from the brigade command ever. I received orders from the battalion command always.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And where did the battalion command receive its orders?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Probably from a superior command, i.e., from the brigade command.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And from whom did the brigade command receive its orders?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Well, according to the military hierarchy, it would be normal for the brigade command to receive its orders from the corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And the corps command in turn received its orders from the Main Staff; correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And the Main Staff received its orders from the president; correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Not necessarily. Not always.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Well, when would it not receive its directions from the president?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: In cases of fierce attacks from the enemy side.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: But the general hierarchy was that the president was over the Main Staff; we can agree with that?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Well, the president, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Right. Now, I'm going to show you a couple of documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could we call up, please, P3042.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: You can see from this document it's dated the 11th of April, 1994. It's from the Main Staff of the VRS and it's addressed to the president of the Republika Srpska, the chief of the Main Staff of the Yugoslav Army, and to the commands of all of the corps, including the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. And if we can turn, please, to the last page of this document, and if we look at the final paragraph mainly to blow it up. It's a little difficult for you to read, Mr. Trapara. We'll blow it up for you.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: I can't see anything. It's very pale. I can't see the letters.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the document has to be rotated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, it's the other way around.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Are you able to read the final paragraph? If you're not, I will read it to you. This document is in evidence already.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: No. Believe me, I can't see a thing. It's upside down, it's blurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'll read it to you. It says: "Following the decision of the Supreme Command of the armed forces of the RS, all relations between the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska with the UN forces commands should be suspended. The restriction of movement for the teams and convoys of UNPROFOR and the humanitarian organisations is still in force." And that was issued by General Milovanovic. Do you agree that's what it says?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: At the bottom I can see Manojlo Milovanovic's name typed up. I can't see a signature, no stamp. It doesn't say in his own hand. There's no stamp. There's no signature.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we ask Mr. Gaynor to provide us information about the date when this document was drafted.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: This document is dated on the front page, 11th of April, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Witness, I'm not actually asking you about the authenticity of this document. What I'm asking you about is the content of the final sentence in it, and that is that there is a restriction on movement of teams and convoys of UNPROFOR and humanitarian organisations in force at the date of this document; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: That's what I see here. That's what it's written. However, I never applied this to be very specific, this ban I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: You acted in direct contravention of orders from the corps command?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: When it comes to this order, I have to say that I could have learned about it through the battalion command. That was the only way for me to be aware of this order, but I never received this order from the battalion commander, nor was I aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: We'll have a look at another order, P879. This one that's coming up is dated almost exactly 11 months later; that's the 11th of March, 1995. You'll see from the header of this document, Mr. Trapara, that it's issued by the Main Staff of the VRS and it is addressed to the president of the Republika Srpska as well as to the commands of all of the corps, including the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps command. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: This is what it says here.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, if we could go to page 3 in the English, please, and under paragraph 6(II) in the B/C/S. I believe it is page 2 in the B/C/S. Now, in that subparagraph which is headed "situation in the territory," could you read out the final sentence, please. Read it out loud.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: "Due to -- due to sniper fire and the death of two girls, until further notice there is a ban on the movement of humanitarian organisations and convoys."

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, you'll accept that this order was directed at the SRK command?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: That's what it says in the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now I -- you were obliged to follow the orders given down the chain of command from the corps command to your unit, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: This was a strict order to prohibit any movement of humanitarian organisations and convoys, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Well, I must say something here with regard to that statement of yours. The only street, Bjelopoljska Street, which passed through Lukavac via Vrace went in the direction of Grbavica. As I stated in my statement, a convoy was stopped by the military police and seven rifles were found in a lorry carrying flour. This was done by the police, but that police was on the strength of the corps. I, as a company commander, did not have a military police unit. It was impossible for me to have it. I stated that water went straight through the zone of responsibility beneath my lines and below the tunnel in Sarajevo. It never happened that there was a shortage of water. Aneks, Hrasno and Sakino [phoen] Naselje were supplied with water all throughout the war. I did not have much influence on convoys.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: But do you accept that there was a policy at the very highest levels of the Bosnian Serb army and at the very highest level of the Bosnian Serb political structures to deliberately obstruct the delivery of humanitarian assistance?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: At that time I was a young man. I was a company commander. I was a local guy. People knew me. And I did not have access to information at such a high level. This was a very high level for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'll bring you to one final document before we finish, that's P3042 -- sorry, pardon me, correction. Could I please have P2479. This document is in English, as you can see. It's to Annan at the United Nations in New York. It's from Akashi at UNPROFOR in Sarajevo, dated the 14th of March, 1995. If we can go now to page 3 in the English. I will read out just two extracts from this, and the first extract is the top of paragraph 6. There it says: "On the subject of freedom of movement, particularly with regard to the delivery of humanitarian assistance, General Mladic was very obstructive. He insisted on absolute parity between what is delivered to the Bosnian Serbs and what is delivered to the enclaves." Now, when we move a little further down in this document it says: "Karadzic, calling Abdic 'an old friend' and 'an intelligent man' said that he (Karadzic) could not let Abdic down by allowing aid to pass through Banja Luka, thereby depriving Abdic of his source of aid." And this discussion arises in the context of UNPROFOR insisting on unimpeded access for humanitarian supplies. So on the basis of what you've -- we've seen so far, do you accept that there was, indeed, a policy at the highest level of the Bosnian Serb army and at the highest level of the Bosnian Serb political organs to deliberately obstruct the delivery of humanitarian assistance?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: I didn't know anything about that at the time. I know Mr. Abdic well, but only from the media like everybody else. I didn't know that things had to be done in the way as is described here.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Trapara.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very briefly. I would like to call up D105 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While we are waiting, Mr. Trapara, could you please tell the Trial Chamber - and the Trial Chamber is not aware of our family names - can you tell what is the ethnicity of my old friend Abdic?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Fikret Abdic is a Bosniak or was a Bosniak, rather.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please look at that decision that I issued on the 7th of May, 1993.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: I'm looking at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does it conform or is it contrary to what you have been told here about obstructions to the flow of humanitarian aid?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: This decision is contrary to what has just been said here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now can we take a look at D690. Could we zoom in on the document. Could I ask you to read the first paragraph if you can.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes, I can: "In order to ensure the normal functioning of humanitarian organisations, the unobstructed passage of all humanitarian aid convoys travelling by road routes and corridors of Republika Srpska organised by the UNHCR, the International Committee of the Red Cross, Medecins Sans Frontieres, Handicap International, the World Health Organisation, the International Rescue Committee."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is this in keeping with what the Prosecutor put to you?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Trapara. I have no further questions for you and I would like to thank you for having come here to provide your evidence.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, that concludes your evidence, Mr. Trapara. On behalf of the Chamber, I thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. Now you are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But we'll rise all together. We'll have a break now, given the time. So we'll break for 45 minutes and resume at ten past 1.00.
