utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellency. I would now like to read out the summary of Mr. Tusevljak's testimony in English. [In English] Slobodan Tusevljak lived on Zagorska Street in Novo Sarajevo before the war broke out. During the war he was a platoon commander of the 1st Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade. Prior to the war, the Serbs who lived on the street were in good terms with their Muslim and Croatian neighbours. They jointly organised mixed neighbourhood watches without any weapons in order to prevent incidents. In January or February 1992 armed Muslims set up barricades at the end of his street and were checking people. Once these barricades were set up, movement in the city was difficult and he could not get to his work-place out of fear for his personal safety. His boss, a Muslim, informed him that if he did not show up to work he would be fired and eventually he was, despite explaining the reasons for his impossibility. Slobodan Tusevljak had no weapons before or in May 1992, when Muslims fired at his houses -- at their houses. The following morning he sent his family away to Tilava and he stayed behind with some neighbours so that they could organise themselves and protect their houses. On this occasion a man brought small arms and distributed them among the group. Before the Muslim attack on June the 8th, 1992, his unit had organised themselves to search houses and found about 30 men. Colonel Dragomir Milosevic gave them the option of going in the depth of the Serb territory or crossing over the Muslim part -- over to the Muslim part of the city, explaining that they could not stay there since it was a war zone. The men were thankful for that option and decided to go to the part of the city under Muslim control. On June the 8th, 1992, Muslims attacked their positions, pushing them back some 200-250 metres. They first attacked with mortars and then with the small arms. His unit had five or six casualties and about ten wounded. From the positions to which they had retreated they watched the Muslim forces setting fire on their houses. After this attack in the line of disengagement remained -- the line of disengagement, the confrontation line remained unchanged until the end of the war. This line was only 10 metres wide in some places -- 10 metres distance from each other. Since the day -- that day, his unit only conducted defensive operations because Muslim forces were constantly attacking their positions which were of vital strategic importance, because otherwise Muslim forces would have had control over the Lukavica-Pale communication route, being able to cut off Grbavica and massacre the civilian population. Muslim forces attacked his zone of responsibility on a daily basis with snipers and mortars and they set fire to civilian houses in the depth of their territory using incendiary fire grenades, killing a large number of women and children. On June the 12th, 1992, Muslim forces launched another attack firing 120-millimetre-calibre mortar mounted on moving railroad cars on the railroad tracks in the Pofalici area. When the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps was formed, his unit became the 1st Platoon of the 4th Company of the 2nd Battalion of the 1st Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade, holding the same positions as before until the end of the war. They only had one 60-millimetre-calibre mortar, but no mortar bombs. The Muslim units opposed to them belonged to 101st Mountain Brigade of the 1st Corps of BH army. His unit was heavily outnumbered; it was comprised of 42 men and at the beginning of the war and was down to 20 men by the end. Around September 1994 Slobodan Tusevljak was so worn out that he decided to hand-over the duty of platoon commander and join, as a common soldier, a neighbouring platoon where attacks were much less intense. They had knowledge that the units of the 1st Corps of BH army had positions in civilian zones and in the depth of their territory. His unit, Mr. Tusevljak's unit, was careful not to target civilian objects and he never allowed anyone to fire at the city or at civilian targets. Never he, or any other members of his unit or their subordinated or superior commands, intended to cause civilian casualties or terrorise civilians in the territory under Muslim control or attack means of public transportation such as trams or buses. They never received or issued any verbal or written orders to that effect. On the contrary, orders and instructions from superior commands were to open fire exclusively at the enemy forces, and only when their positions were under attack and to defend their lives and the line of defence. If an enemy soldier was captured, he would be handed over to the company command. With regard to sniping incidents -- to sniping incident in Ivana Krndelja Street on 3rd of September, 1993, Slobodan Tusevljak states that no line of sight existed between their positions and the scene of the alleged incident. With regard to sniping incident in Miljenka Cvitkovica Street in the Cengic Vila area on 22nd of July, 1994, Slobodan Tusevljak states that no line of sight existed between their positions and the scene. Moreover, the distance between that spot and their positions was over 1.200 metres and they had no weapons with that kind of range or snipers in the rank of his unit. Due to the constant attack on Ozrenska Street and Grbavica by Muslim snipers positioned behind Muslim lines on Asimovo Brdo, by the end of 1993 a trained sniper was sent to his unit. His target was in the opposite direction of the city. This sniper was killed two days later and after this no more snipers arrived in his unit. [Interpretation] Could we now have a look at 1D6090. Could we have that document on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While waiting for it to appear, Mr. Tusevljak, what was the ethnic composition of your settlement?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Well, it was mixed. There was Serbs, there were Muslims, there were Croats. The majority consisted of Serbs, but there were also Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell the Chamber what happened to the non-Serb population and what happened to the Serbs as well? What happened when it came to remaining there or leaving?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Some people left their homes immediately after the barricades had been set up at night. They left, they went to town. Some remained. That was the situation. People, quite simply, left; and those who remained, remained in their houses until the fighting started.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were the Serbs duty-bound to respond to the call-up?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Yes. It was said that we had to be mobilised, that we had to join up, to form some sort of an army, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did this also concern non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We wanted to show this document, this list. This is your platoon from the 4th Company; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is there a list of weapons that your platoon had included in this list?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What does this mean, an automatic rifle or a semi-automatic rifle?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Yes, AP means automatic rifle, PAP means semi-automatic rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What's the name of this person under number 11? You don't have to read it.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Himzo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You don't have to tell us his name. What's his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Are there any Croats?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Yes. Under number 5, let me just have a look, number 16, then there is also number 20. There were others probably or I'm sure of that, in fact, but this list isn't quite complete, the list of these platoon members.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were their families in the same settlement?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: They were in the settlement or in the rear Lukavica-Tilava. They went there to -- so as not to be on the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was this document --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Has this document been admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have English translation for this?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not yet. I do apologise. We don't have a translation yet, but we're concerned with the names and the names of rifles. Our only purpose was to see what sort of weapons the platoon had. That was our sole intention. So the translation would not be any different from the list that we have here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Tusevljak, could you kindly read out the first line aloud.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "A list of the weapons of the 1st Platoon of the 4th Company."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. And what does the letter on the right side at number 5 mean "Zbrojovka-Brno"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that's the Croat who received an automatic rifle. He wanted a high-calibre weapon, so he got a "Zrbojovka-Brno" which is an old Czech weapon, something similar to a machine-gun. It's a Czech-made weapon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objection, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it we do not need the translation for this at the moment. Yes, we'll admit it in full.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D2396.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I said we'll admit it in full. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see 6091 -- 1D6091, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tusevljak, could you please mark this document or tell us whether there are Muslims and Croats included here and under which numbers. You don't have to read out the names.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Number 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And number 5?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: I apologise. I skipped number 5. Number 5, number 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What is the ethnicity of the person under 5?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Muslim, it's a Muslim under 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: He was wounded, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Yes. Number 6 is a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. Could we scroll up. Have a look to see if there are any others.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Well, probably but this list isn't a complete one either.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: There are some to the right, some names to the right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that. Perhaps we could scroll down a bit to see the ones below.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. Could we scroll down a little more.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could we see the next page. Who was under number 90?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Number 90, a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And number 98?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Number 98, he is a Croat, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: 96 is also a Croat, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. What about number 73?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: He's also a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we briefly have a look at the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What is the ethnicity of the last person listed?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: No. Beneath that.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: A Croat. He turned up a little later so his name was added rapidly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What about 116, could that be a Serb?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure. I don't know this person.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we just have a look at the first page so that you can identify the nature of this list. Could you read out the first line. What is this list?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: This is a list of combatants from the 4th Company of the 2nd Battalion. The date is the 18th of February, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this please be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, this will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D2397, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. At this stage we have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tusevljak, as you noted, your evidence in chief was admitted in writing in lieu of your oral testimony. Now you'll be cross-examined by the member of the Prosecution. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Hello again, Mr. Tusevljak.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And thank you for meeting with me yesterday.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you eventually some questions about some of the things we spoke about yesterday, but right now I'd just like to pick up on a couple of answers you've given to Dr. Karadzic. When you mentioned barricades in your first answers, what barricades were you talking about?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Well, those were Muslim barricades at the end of our street. The barricades were erected on their side where they had a majority, from our street in the direction of the city. And then in January and February they controlled who was passing by. They were armed. So us men did not dare go in the direction of the city. We didn't go to work. We would send our wives to go and buy something because a majority of the stores and shops were in the city.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So, Mr. Tusevljak, I'd just like to try and place this in time a little bit more specifically. Are you sure you're talking about something in January or February, or are you talking about the barricades that were erected throughout Sarajevo on March 1st and 2nd after the referendum?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: No, no. The barricades were erected before that. I knew those men very well. They were criminals. That area below our street, I knew a guy whose nickname was Rus. In any case, most of them were criminals. They erected the barricades, and they stopped passers-by and obviously they had weapons. They were armed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you're talking about a very localised incident then?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Right below my street.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. The other question I want to ask you -- well, I'll put it this way. Dr. Karadzic asked you whether Serbs were duty-bound to respond to the call-up. And what call-up did you understand Dr. Karadzic to be referring to?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: When the war started we had to organise ourselves. To put it simply, us people wanted to organise ourselves. We wanted people to respond to a mobilisation call and join a Serbian army that would be there to defend us, to defend ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So who made the call-up?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Well, people organised themselves. That's how things were in my street. The guys set up a company command and they selected the rest of us. We were going to be combatants. They wanted us to organise ourselves. I suppose that those guys had been in the military before. I don't know. They just invited us to organise ourselves, to set up units in order to be able to defend ourselves because down in the city units had already been organised. We saw it on TV. We saw the Patriotic League and all of the other units. We saw the reserve police --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Who -- who invited you to organise ourselves?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: My neighbours who were perhaps up there. They represented somebody from the local commune. They were activists.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Would that be somebody from the Serb local commune or somebody from the Muslim local commune?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: It was a mixed local commune. I was one of the activists in that mixed local commune; however, when the first barricades were erected we divided. Us Serbs lived up and the others lived below. Those people had worked with me before. The Serbs remained on one side, Muslim stayed on the other side. I knew people who had been activists before and worked in the local commune on various issues.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And just to go back to the question I asked you in a more detailed way, who in particular invited you to organise yourselves? Can you give us a name?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. There was a man in the company, Vito Kapuran. He was also an activist in the local commune. I suppose that they organised themselves in Lukavica and they invited us to do the same, to organise ourselves, to be provided with weapons if necessary to be able to defend our lives, to defend our homes, that is. I remember him.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And that would have been through the Crisis Staffs at that time, wouldn't it have?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Yes, I suppose. As I've told you, I was at home. I had young children so I did not get engaged too much. I suppose that there was a Crisis Staff in Lukavica I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. And then one more thing that Dr. Karadzic went through, if we could see D2396 again, please. It's the first document that he showed you. I'd like just to have another quick look at this document and perhaps you can tell us about a couple of the other weapons that are set out here on this list so that we know what your platoon had. I see a number 9, a number 21, and if we could go over to the next page, please -- oh, the next page looks like it might be a duplicate of the first page. So if we can go back. So number 9 and 21 on the first page are people who have M84 weapons. Could you tell us what those are?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: It's a machine-gun, M84. It's a machine-gun. It's a new model different from what it used to be before. It's an infantry weapon. I suppose that each platoon had one or two such pieces.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And what calibre of bullets did they use?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: 7.62, I think. There may be a slight difference. I don't remember exactly, but I believe that I'm right.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. How about we just go down the list a minute to number 23. Somebody there has got an M53. What's that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: It's a PM, it's another machine-gun. What I'm reading here is PM. It's a machine-gun, M53, an old light machine-gun also known as Sarac, and the calibre of its bullet is 7.9. It's an old piece of weaponry.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. We can remove that document and move on then. Now yesterday you confirmed to me - as Dr. Karadzic has just said - you were platoon commander for the 1st Platoon of the 4th Company of the 2nd Battalion of the 1st Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade. Now, your brigade commander at that time was Veljko Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: He was the battalion commander, not the brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Who was the commander of the brigade?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: I don't remember, believe me. Perhaps it was Milosevic, but I'm not sure. I don't know much about any of the superior commands. I don't know who the commanders were at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And how many companies were in your battalion?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: I believe that there were five companies.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And who was your battalion commander?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: There were several. First it was Stojanovic, then he got killed, and the last one was Aco Petrovic. I don't remember of those who were in between. People got killed or were redeployed or reappointed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you also told me yesterday the names of some of your company commanders, including Savo Vukovic, Rajko Ciro, Dusan Zorovac, Sinisa Jeremic, a relative of yours, Zeljko Tusevljak, and Dusan Loncaric.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Zeljko, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your battalion command was on Banja Lucka Street in Grbavica and your company command headquarters was on Ozrenska Street.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Each company had its own ammunition storage; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And who supplied it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: I don't know. Our superior command. I don't have a clue. Weapons came from a higher instance, from the brigade perhaps. I don't know. We were issued with the weapons and ammunition from the company commander from our -- for our platoon. How he obtained weapons, I don't know, perhaps from the brigade, from the brigade command.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: How did you get your orders?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Verbally, from the company commander. He would give orders to me as the platoon commander. He told me what our tasks and duties would be for every given day.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So that means you saw him every day to get those orders; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, just to go on to another section of your statement, you said at paragraph 7 that you personally had no weapons until May of 1992, and yesterday you told me that in May you received a 7.62-calibre automatic rifle.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: I forgot to tell you yesterday that I was first issued with a semi-automatic weapon, then an automatic weapon. In May I got the semi-automatic and then it was replaced by the automatic rifle. You have to know that we did not have that many pieces. Vito Kapuran was the commander of the platoon before me. I was just a foot soldier at that time. But he was wounded sometime in the summer and then I was appointed commander either in June or July of that year, of 1992 I mean.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. Just to go back to what I was asking you about. This semi-automatic weapon you said yesterday that you got it from the command. What command were you talking about?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: The 4th Company. That command was set up in a house and that was the command for that area, the command of that company. They invited me to come up there, to issue me with a weapon, and first they gave me a semi-automatic weapon. That was in Ozrenska beyond the defence lines. This is where I was issued with my first piece of weaponry.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness said that he was invited to be issued with a weapon because he had a military obligation and that was never recorded on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Can you confirm, Mr. Tusevljak, that that's what you said?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. And you also said that your Serbian neighbours had small arms. What did you mean by "small arms"?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Those were semi-automatic and automatic rifles and even M48 rifles. Those were old rifles. That would be that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And where did they get them?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: They got them -- I don't know how they got them. It was not a well-known and well advertised fact. They were hiding that. I believe that they got them in February because fire came from the city and they got them. I don't know how because I did not have any.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And what about this man you referred to in your statement referred to as Vito who got additional small arms. What did he bring?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: He -- I was told that Vito came to the command where the company command was set up and he brought light weaponry, rifles, both semi-automatic and automatic rifles and grenades. I don't know who Vito was. I only know that I was told that his name was Vito, some Vito.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So this information is not information that you personally -- that you came upon that you saw; it's second-hand information?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Yes. We were told to come up there because he had brought weaponry. Since we had our military obligation, we were supposed to be issued with those weapons so as to be able to organise ourselves. That's why we were invited to go up there, to be issued with weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And when in May did this happen, do you remember?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: I don't understand. When you say when did this happen, what do you mean? What is this?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: When in the month of May did you get this invitation that you've just been speaking about? When in May did you get the invitation?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: In early May, I believe, at the beginning of May or thereabouts. That's when my religious holiday is. It was after my religious holiday. It was either on the 8th, 9th, or the 10th, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So at this command where you went to collect your weapons, did you see anybody in uniform?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: No, we still wore civilian clothes. Nobody had a uniform. There was a man, the 1st Company commander, who had a camouflage uniform. But I believe that it had been made from a tent. That's how the first uniforms were obtained.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So when you talk about the arms that you and your neighbours received, you're again talking about a very, very localised experience as I understand it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 11 of your statement you said that after June 8th, 1992, your unit only conducted defensive operations because Muslim forces were constantly attacking your positions. So I have a couple of questions about that. The first question is: Do you accept that these attacks were with a view to unblocking the city of Sarajevo from its siege?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Well, no. I don't think that would be the case. It had nowhere to go from there even if they had succeeded in that because all of that was a Serb territory. The only reason may have been to interrupt the Pale-Lukavica road so we would not be able to function. Further on, in depth everything else was a Serb territory, there were no Muslims there, so I don't know why they would want to even go there in the first place. There were no Muslims there, at least not in that area.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Would it be of any assistance for -- to offer the witness a hard copy of his statement if the Prosecutor is going to refer paragraphs in his statement.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Karadzic repeat the exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: We can offer it if it is convenient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it there's no objection, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Oh, of course not, but I just don't have one in Mr. Tusevljak's language, so I hope Dr. Karadzic has one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think we can print it out. Please continue, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So, Mr. Tusevljak, you don't really know then that the attack on June 8th that you referred to was part of a larger operation on two simultaneous fronts from inside the city and Bosnian positions outside the city, with a view to unblocking it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: No, no, I don't know. They launched attacks, but I did not see any purpose of those attacks. Even if they had succeeded, I don't know what they would have gained, at least not in that part. There would be no communication with the rest of their territory because everything beyond that -- there was Serbian territory, save for that road. If they had cut off Grbavica, Grbavica would have remained in a horseshoe and that's the only thing that they could have cut off, the only part of our territory in the city. That's the way I see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, just about your assertion that your unit only conducted defensive operations, I want to show you a couple of documents that relate specifically to your area. The first one is P1478 and it's the handwritten notebook of General Mladic, and the page number in the B/C/S transcript is page -- your indulgence for a moment. I think it's page 240 and in English it's page 241. In English pages 241/242, actually. Now in B/C/S can you go back to page 240. Keep going back. I see when I was sent this information I wasn't sent the e-court numbers; I was sent the actual document numbers. The English page that you had on the screen is right, page 241. I'll move on. Let's go to 65 ter number 23749. This is an order for further operations dated 9 October 1992 signed by General Galic. And if we can go over to paragraph 5.3 in both documents, please. Now, among the operations set out in this document is one that you see in paragraph 5.3 specifically impacts on your area. It calls for the Romanija Infantry Brigade to create conditions to take over a wider area of Asimovo Brdo (Hrasno) which would - and if you can go over to the next page in English, please - which would secure favourable positions on the left wing and expansion of the territory in the area around Pero Kosuric square. Now, Mr. Tusevljak, I have a hard time understanding your assertion that you only conducted defensive operations in the face of this document.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: On one occasion there was the intention to attack Hasim hill. As I said, it was behind our backs. It was behind us. They fired on us with snipers from Asimovo hill so we couldn't operate, quite simply. So the intention was to attack that hill and take that part of the territory but this was never done, and the situation remained such until the end of the war. That initial position, the position they used for the first attacks, remained right until the end. The lines were such that they were. We were supposed to do this, but we didn't. I don't know why. We were never issued an order of any kind to do this. We were supposed to do this. We should have done this for our own sake, in order to ensure we were safe, but this was never done and the lines remained as they were up until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, if we can try again to go back to General Mladic's notebook, P1478. On 27 June 1992 - and I'll read to you what he said - in a meeting at Lukavica at 1550 in the afternoon, ten minutes to 4.00, a meeting with the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps commander, General Mladic noted: "Operations to take Hrasno Asimovo hill elevation 648 are underway, and in the 1st Romanija Brigade nice soldiers were killed and 11 wounded." So it seems an operation like that did get underway even earlier on.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Well, I'm not aware of that. We were at the foot of Asimovo hill. Whether they attacked or our people, I don't know. We were at the foot. We didn't move anywhere. But I know that no one moved. The situation remained as it was. Fire was opened, that's all. I think I would be informed if our men had attacked but I don't think they did because something would have been moved, the lines would have been moved, but the situation remained the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Let's go to paragraph 12 of your statement. There you talked about Muslim forces firing mortars -- firing from mortars mounted on railway cars, on railway tracks in the Pofalici area. And you said in your statement you responded to the attack with support from the rear. And I wonder if you can tell me how you knew that they were firing from railway cars since you actually wouldn't be able to see that from your positions.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Well, most of my information was obtained from Serbs who had crossed over from Muslim territory to our side. This happened on a weekly basis or on a monthly basis. Someone would flee from down there in the town and come over to our side, and then naturally they told us about everything, because they lived down there and they knew about everything. Most of the information we obtained was from people who continued to flee.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you said you responded to the attack with support from the rear. How did you respond?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Well, on that occasion I personally called the company commander. I said that we were under attack, that we were being fired on with mortar shells behind our company, in the depth. This was at the beginning, I think. Some sort of a mortar unit had been established and I think that they had 60- and 82-millimetre mortars. He called them and they took action. They tried to return fire in front of our positions, but they hit both us and them. Later I called them again and told them that they weren't helping us because it was so close that they couldn't take action because we were being hit as well as their lines. Our shells were hitting us as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: How often did that sort of thing happen?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: You mean the attacks; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That shells from your forces would hit you as well?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Whenever there was an attack of any kind, if we called up and asked for mortar support, on such occasions we had to take shelter because we knew that we could be hit because the lines were so close to each other. So it all depended on the attack launched by the Muslim forces against our forces. In such cases we would take shelter to the extent that this was possible. Some would remain behind in order to open fire. In order to put an end to that artillery attack whether it was their attack or our attack, they probably acted in a similar way because the lines were very close to each other so the artillery was not of much assistance to us at all and we rarely asked for their help.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So let's go back to the train cars for a second or the railway cars for a second. If you only found out from people who had crossed over to your side that the fire had been coming from railway cars in the Pofalici area, how did you know exactly what to shoot at?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Well, they told us where they were firing on us -- from which positions they were firing on us, but we fired in front of us. We weren't interested in the mortar attacks. Someone else was interested in that. We told the command where they were opening fire from, but our mortars fired in front of us, on the infantry in front of us, on the area in front of our lines, not down there. Down there is far away. They couldn't target that area.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, who was interested in the mortar attacks then?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: I don't understand. What do you mean who was interested in --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, you've just said, "We weren't interested in the mortar attacks. Someone else was interested in that."

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Well, we would report to the company commander, tell him where the mortars were firing from, and he would probably convey this to the battalion commander. He would probably provide the battalion commander with that information.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So when we're talking about what you've written in paragraph 12 of your statement that Muslim forces launched an attack firing from mortars on railway tracks in the depth of your territory, that's actually an attack that you don't know -- you don't yourself know where it was launched from. And you don't know then what targets your forces would be responding to?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Well, look. The attack took place on the 12th. After the 12th, the people who turned up told us where they were opening fire from. I was there in my house. First they did all of that with mortars and then the infantry attacked, but they weren't able to penetrate on that occasion. We had men who were killed and wounded, quite a lot of them on that occasion. They also took some Croats captive, and so on and so forth. I was there myself. I know that these were 120-millimetre shells, and there was shrapnel. Later when these people turned up they said where they were firing from. They were firing on our positions from those positions --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: -- that's certain. We informed the command of this fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So, Mr. Tusevljak --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The response hasn't been recorded correctly in the transcript, the end of the response. It was said that -- it's been corrected now, yes, that they informed the brigade of the location from which fire was being opened. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we continue?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So when you said in your statement that you took care not to fire at civilians, this doesn't actually sound like an example of you taking care. This is second-hand information on targets that weren't identified in civilian areas, and you only heard about whether or not targets had been attained after the fact.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have a reference. Which paragraph is it?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: We're still talking about paragraph 12.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you said in your statement -- what Dr. Karadzic is looking for is where you said you were careful not to target civilian objects in the zone of responsibility of the ABiH 1st Corps. That's at paragraph 19. So how is that taking care, Mr. Tusevljak? Second-hand information about targets that weren't clearly identified, and you only heard about whether or not those targeted had been attained after the fact.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Well, look, we didn't open fire on those positions. We didn't have any weapons with which we could fire on Pofalici. That was far away from our lines. Our mortars when they provided us with support, they fired in front of us, 10 or 15 metres in front of us, directly at their lines. They were attacking us. We never fired on Pofalici. My unit never did that. We had no equipment to do this with. We just reported as to where they were firing from. People told us that they were opening fire from mortars on us from such and such positions. But we didn't have anything we could use to retaliate. We only had infantry weapons. We fought in an area of 20, 30, or 50 metres. It would be silly for us to fire on the town when the enemy was right in front of us. We couldn't have fired on the town. To protect the positions would have been impossible. We had these odd weapons. It was very close. We just reported to the battalion command, the company command, on location from which these mortars were opening fire. As to whether they took any measures or not --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: -- I do not know --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Let's move on then.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The transcript does not reflect the fact that the witness said we did not open fire in order to make sure that our positions were not detected.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, in your statement at paragraph 25 you were -- you indicated you were briefed about some sniping incidents that you referred to as F4 and F10, and you said that no line of sight existed between your positions and the scene of the alleged incident. But, Mr. Tusevljak, your company was spread along a line that ran part of the length of Ozrenska Street and you indicated that to me yesterday.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Yes, but it was below Ozrenska Street. Ozrenska Street was the closest road but it was 150 to 200 metres below. That's a hill. So it was beneath Ozrenska Street. Ozrenska is further up.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Let's have a look at a photo from Ozrenska Street of the location of sniping incident F4 among other things. It's 65 ter number 23968. So, Mr. Tusevljak, this photo of the transversal to the corner where sniping incident F4 took place was taken from Ozrenska Street in the year 2000. Do you see a line of sight?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Well, I don't know where this is, but yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Let's go on to 65 ter number 23967.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown the site of the incident.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, on a map.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is this from the street or is it in the depth? You can't see the street --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, if necessary, you can take up the matter in your re-examination. Please don't interrupt Ms. Edgerton in her cross-examination. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, this is from -- this photo is taken from the same location with a little bit of a zoom on the very same day. And the scene -- sorry? Did you want to say something?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I want to say that it's only now I can see where this is. This is to the right. This is Ozrenska Street but further down below. My platoon was to the right, or rather, to the left, far to the left, so this can't have been --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And what platoon of your company held the territory to the right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Well, I think it was -- well, there was the 5th -- I think it was the 2nd Company. I was the 4th Company. Now I know where this is. But it certainly wasn't from our positions. We were far to the left, quite far away. So this isn't it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So your issue then is -- or what you assert then is that from the specific positions of your platoon there was no line of sight to the transversal where this particular sniping incident occurred, but you also agree that there's a very clear line of sight from further along Ozrenska Street to either the point where the 2nd or I think you said the 5th Platoon was operational?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: No, the 2nd, the 2nd, not the 5th, the 2nd Company, not platoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And do you know who the commander was of the 2nd Company?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Well, believe me I don't. I think it was some -- well, I've forgotten. Could it have been -- well, I can't remember, believe me.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now let's go to sniping incident F10 and 65 ter number 24007. And we're going to look at a photograph from the other direction, from the incident location up to Ozrenska Street. So the young woman -- pardon me, the young boy and the woman that you see in this picture are standing immediately adjacent to the location of this sniping incident. Can you see the hilltop where Ozrenska Street sits in the distance? And this photo, by the way, was also taken in the year 2000.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I can see it somewhere up there.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So let's go to 24008, which is a photograph taken from the same location with a zoom, where you can see Ozrenska Street positions even clearer; wouldn't you agree?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Yes. But again, that's not it. I was to the right of this cafe. I know this more or less, but I wasn't there believe me. We were further up in the direction of Mojmilo, in the direction of the Asimovo hill, but this was farther away in the direction of Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And who was there?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Well, our battalion, that same company, the 2nd or 1st. I don't know how far the area extended. Below us there was the 1st, 2nd, 3rd, 4th, we were the 4th, and then there was the 5th on Mojmilo, the 5th -- or the person who testified before me was from the 5th Company, then there was myself and we were far away in the direction of Mojmilo.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now just with respect to this incident, sniping incident F10, you also said you had no weapons with a range that would enable you to hit a spot 1200 metres away. So now we've just seen a document at the outset of your cross-examination here, D2397, that shows that your platoon had, among other things, M84 machine-guns. Do you know what the effective range is for an M84?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Yes, that machine-gun has a range, but the two machine-guns were further back in the rear and they protected us. So one of them was in a clearing and was only used to protect that clearing, that line. You need sights to have a line of sight. I don't think you can hit anything from such a distance, but it was prohibited to fire on the town because I was the commander and I prohibited that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Tusevljak --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: I had two sisters. I had my friends and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I just asked you a question about what the effective range is for an M84. If you could just focus on that, that would be great.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: I believe that this is the range, but you have to have optical sights in order to hit something at that distance. But we didn't have that. We just had the machine-gun as any other infantry unit. We had a machine-gun.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And what about an M53 that we also saw in D2396, do you know what the effective range is for an M53?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: It's very similar, but it doesn't have optical sights. It just fires bursts of fire. It can't fire an individual bullet, neither the previous one nor this one. Those are machine-guns, you know, but I believe that the range is similar.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And then just one last question and it relates to paragraph 26 in your statement. You said at the end of 1993 a trained sniper was sent to your unit whose task was to eliminate the Muslim sniper on Asimovo Brdo and after this no other snipers arrived in your unit. So in that regard I'd like to -- like us to have a look at P5945. It's a document from Vlado Lizdek, who eventually became the commander of the 1st Romanija Infantry Brigade to General Galic and it's dated 29 October 1993. Now, in the second-to-last paragraph on this document which you see in full on the page on the left and we have to go over to page 2 in the English document. It's -- the first sentence is actually at the bottom of page 1. In this document Colonel Lizdek reports to General Galic that his brigade has a total of 68 sniper rifles of different calibres, but he says at the bottom of the page that in the earlier period a sniper group of the 1st Romanija Brigade's military police platoon was active around Grbavica. And that seems to suggest something to the contrary of what you assert in paragraph 25.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Well, listen. The area of Grbavica, that was far from us. It had nothing whatsoever to do with my unit. Grbavica is quite a way from us. I don't know about Grbavica, but I can talk about my company. I can tell you that we were far from Grbavica. If you have a map you will see where Grbavica is as opposed to us. I don't know about Grbavica. I never went there. You only went there when you had to because of the snipers. We didn't have any sharpshooters, save for that one who arrived and he was killed. He was a sharpshooter. That was the only one.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Edgerton. Mr. Karadzic, do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Excellencies. Very brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tusevljak, may I ask you this: On the 3rd of September, 1993, was fire opened from Ozrenska Street on civilians in the city?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: No, no. As far as I know for my part no fire was opened. There was a ban on that. It was prohibited, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Therefore, does that also imply Ivana Krndelja Street?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That street is below us a bit to the right. That's where my elementary school is. I know where it is, but you couldn't see it that well because there was a hill between us. You could only see the bridge at the bottom of that street. We didn't have good visibility of that street.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On the 22nd of July, 1994, was fire opened on civilians in Miljenka Cvitkovica Street?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: No, no, again that is far. The first one was closer and the latter one is far. I don't think so. My platoon, my troops, didn't fire. The entire company did not open fire. Muslims were so close that we were afraid to reveal ourselves to them. People were 20 metres away from us. We didn't dare fire at them or on the city. It was very -- it was very dangerous to reveal your positions. We were below the foundations of the houses. We did not dare leave the houses. We didn't dare go out to see what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 12 , the last sentence, can you read it, please. Can you read it out loud.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: "We returned fire because we received support from our rear."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is that that? When you said "we returned fire," it was not your unit but a unit at a higher level from the rear?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Yes, yes, because we called them. We told them that we were being shelled and that an infantry attack would ensue and we asked for assistance. We wanted them to shell in front of the lines at the infantry that was attacking us. We did not know where the attack came from. Subsequently we learned that it was from Pofalici and from that general area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Those units that had artillery mortar group, did they have the means to observe fire?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Yes. Some observers did come up there and they could observe the situation. They had the means obviously.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I don't know what the number was, but Ms. Edgerton called up Mladic's diary on Tuesday, 16 June 1992, where a meeting is described. It is page 171 in the Serbian version. The Colonel briefed the others about combat. There were no questions. And he says they are launching attacks on the Bosut facility and Ozrenska Street. Does this tally with what you know? What does it mean when he says attacks came in waves?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Yes, that's what their attacks were like. An attack would last for a whole day or even two days. When they attacked, there was no stopping them. It was continuous. They had quite a lot of men. They could take turns and, for example, that attack on the 8th lasted for two, three days, and then there was a break of one day and then they continued on the 12th. And all the other attacks were very similar. There was a pattern along the length of the line and they were looking for a place where to break through the line especially in my zone of responsibility. That's what they were targeting the most.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: My last question: You were asked about the mobilisation call-ups. Who was it who issued that? Was there a representative of the Ministry of Defence in the municipality?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Yes, there was one.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, he's done it more than once now, actually, probably something more like about seven times, but these are completely leading questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Absolutely. Are you through, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes. I'll give up on any other questions that I may have had.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tusevljak, thank you very much for having come here to testify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That concludes your evidence, Mr. Tusevljak. Thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. Now you're free to go. But we'll rise all together. It's very difficult to follow the order of witnesses with this pace. I take it the witness we will hear tomorrow is Mr. Gray?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And after him, who?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Simic. Thank you. The hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 8th day of November, 2012, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.46 p.m.,
